transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
On the eve of midterm election day,
President Trump delivered his closing message
for Republicans at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
We've done a great job here, though.
The people from interior have been incredible,
and the pool is now better and more beautiful
than it's ever been before.
The president spent some 20 minutes
talking about his renovation projects
in the nation's capital
before casting Democrats as dangerous radicals.
Tens of millions of Americans
have already cast an early or absentee ballot.
One of the most closely watched races
is in Texas, where Democrat James Talarico
is in a tight race against Republican Ken Paxton.
Steve Futterman reports from Austin.
In his final campaign event,
James Talarico called out to his supporters here in Austin.
There's that moment when you have to leave it all on the field.
Austin, we are in that moment.
1994 was the last time a Democrat
won a statewide election in Texas.
That makes this Talarico supporter,
Gasper Castellanos, a bit nervous.
I am hopeful, but I also am a lifelong Texan,
so I do hold a little bit of just, like, reality.
Ken Paxton made his final campaign stop just north of Dallas.
We have never been this close to losing everything that we hold dear.
Our jobs, our livelihoods, our way of life in Texas.
This is one of a number of races
that will determine control of the U.S. Senate.
For NPR News, I'm Steve Futterman in Austin.
Federal safety investigators say the weather
will be a major focus of the investigation
into Sunday's crash of a business jet in South Florida.
The National Transportation Safety Board says rain pounded the region Sunday
and one of the pilots reported ice conditions at a high altitude.
The NTSB said Monday that evidence found at the crash site
indicated that the aircraft started to break up in the air.
Nine people were killed.
Apple reports strong earnings in its latest quarter,
but its share price got dinged
because the company forecast supply chain constraints
and high memory chip prices ahead.
Embarrassed Jon Ruich reports from Silicon Valley.
Apple's revenue in the September quarter rose 12% year-on-year,
hitting a quarterly record and beating Wall Street's expectations.
But in recent months, the company has been forced to raise prices
on several products because the cost of memory chips has been soaring
as demand from AI data centers skyrockets.
On a call with analysts, Apple executives said they expect
that pressure to continue into the next quarter.
Apple's share price dropped by as much as 4.5%
in after-hours trading before rebounding a bit.
Jon Ruich, NPR News.
U.S. Special Envoy Steve Whitcoff says the U.S. will mediate talks
between Ukraine and Russia next week,
and a social media post Whitcoff said the talks will take place in Abu Dhabi.
You're listening to NPR News.
New York State has reported its first death linked to measles
in more than 30 years.
State health officials said Monday that a child died
in rural Lewis County in northern New York.
The death comes as the U.S. experiences its worst measles resurgence
in decades.
Pennsylvania has been the epicenter of the outbreak,
reporting more than 1,400 confirmed cases
and five measles-associated deaths so far this year.
Electric bikes and electric scooters can be convenient modes
of transportation in urban areas,
but they can also be dangerous, especially for children.
NPR's Rachel Karls reports on a new study
that finds rates of e-bike and scooter injuries are rising
in children and teens across the country.
Brain injuries were twice as common among kids injured on e-bikes
and e-scooters compared to their non-motorized counterparts.
And 8% of patients with e-bike injuries had major problems
or needed ICU-level care.
That's twice the rate of high-severity injuries
versus non-motorized bikes.
The data comes from the medical records of over 13,000 young people
treated for bike, scooter, and skateboard injuries
at six large U.S. pediatric hospitals over the course of three years.
The results were published Monday in JAMA.
Rachel Carlson, NPR News.
More than 20 years after launch, NASA's Swift Observatory
expected to reenter Earth's atmosphere on Wednesday.
The observatory weighs 3,200 pounds
and was designed to study some of the universe's most powerful explosions.
NASA says most of it will burn up as it travels through the atmosphere.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: President Trump delivers closing message for Republicans at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on election eve
Texas Senate race between James Talarico and Ken Paxton tightens in final campaign push
NTSB says weather will be a major focus in investigating Sunday's business jet crash in South Florida
Apple posts record September quarter revenue but warns of memory chip cost pressures
Steve Witkoff says U.S. will mediate Ukraine-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi next week
New York reports its first measles-linked death in over 30 years, a child in Lewis County
Study finds e-bike and e-scooter injuries rising among children, with more brain injuries than non-motorized bikes
NASA's Swift Observatory expected to reenter Earth's atmosphere Wednesday, mostly burning up
